method.outer_pacing: SO_MAX_PACING_RATE on only the authenticated replacement carrier; 2x its observed probe delivery rate for 0.5s; restore previous limit
method.inner_cc: diagnostic only: change the controlled HTTP sender to CUBIC for 5s, restore BBR; no system-wide setting and no socket reconnect
method.receiver_clock: router realtime clock paired with /proc/uptime, using floating-point nanosecond conversion; nominal receiver sampling about 0.1s; no independent sub-millisecond clock-offset qualification
method.confirmation: observed cumulative-byte endpoints wholly after writer admission; no interpolation across sample gaps

limitations: One pair per 5-second/15-second warmup group; not a statistically qualified speedup.
A zero notsent queue at two snapshots does not exclude short bursts or prove that a pacing cap never binds.
Changing the controlled application sender algorithm is a causal diagnostic, not a VPN feature for arbitrary remote TCP senders.
This is recovery under an artificial per-outer-flow policer, not maximum VPN throughput or proof of an ISP loss mechanism.
excluded_attempts: control1: integer nanosecond conversion made sub-second clock mapping invalid; excluded from timing comparison.
pace1: ambiguous uncommitted/stalled socket was safely rejected by the observer; no pacing applied, excluded as an intervention.
initial control3 launch: completed transient systemd unit had already unloaded; runner stopped before creating a test, excluded and retried.
decision: No transport acceleration patch enabled: the measured outer-pacing gain in one-second confirmation is about one receiver sample and is not a qualified repeatable improvement. Commit the measurement admission and evidence instead of a default traffic limiter.
findings: A fresh outer carrier retained a large congestion window after its idle drain wait; the observed trace did not support adding keep-warm cover traffic.

During slow recovery the outer carrier had capacity above the useful delivery rate while the controlled inner BBR sender had a low bandwidth/pacing estimate. This localizes at least part of the reproduced post-admission ramp to the inner sender.

Observed one-second recovery confirmation: control2/pace2 3.854/3.745s; control3/pace3 2.461/2.402s. These differences are comparable to the receiver sampling interval, with one pair per warmup condition.

Switching only the controlled HTTP sender to CUBIC temporarily yielded a 1.141s confirmation after admission, versus 2.461s in its 15-second-warmup control. The same peer and full uninterrupted body were preserved, and BBR was restored. This single diagnostic supports the inner-sender explanation but is not an estimate of general VPN speedup.
